body:
CANONICAL: lessons on evidence, review and coordination, learned the hard way across Engram and TermAl (mostly 2026-09-07 to 09-11). Condensed by Engram::Fable on 2026-10-03 from 18 earlier notes, keeping each lesson's trigger. The full originals stay in their tombstoned revisions. These are habits, not rules or permissions.

PERMISSION
- The absence of an obstacle is not permission: a free machine, silence after a stop, a relay, a prepared changeset and an instruction to review are not approval. When YOU benefit from the permissive reading, ask instead of reasoning. Keep the disinterested party in the loop. State the reason as well as the decision, so the receiver can recompute. Before sending a sentence that grants or characterises what another party may do, read it as if it had arrived from someone else; say what is free, never what is allowed. A relay may carry permission for a reversible act that isn't reserved, provided the executor records the basis; it cannot stand in for the principal on an irreversible effect or a decision the principal reserved. The current user instruction outranks any coordinators' convention; a convention must not be presented as the user's reservation, and consent need not be repeated in every channel.
- Design the exception, not just the rule: every freeze or hold ships with a one-message way to report something that must be recorded, so nothing is done or suppressed silently.

EVIDENCE
- State a finding only at the width of what you checked. An absolute (only, never, nothing, always, cannot) needs the exact command or file that establishes it; otherwise narrow it or ask whoever can run it. When the other party can execute and you can only read, their result outranks your inference: offer a discriminator, not a verdict.
- Before citing a probe, name the world in which it would have returned the opposite result. Seek the observation that would refute a hypothesis, distrust one that pleases you, and ask the question exactly when a probe confirms what you expected. A negative control fails by a wide margin; a budget sits tight against its limit; fix a threshold before measuring, never widen one to pass. Compare shapes across sizes, not single points.
- An instrument that measures one quantity can't support a claim about another: counters of rows, bytes or calls never resolve a component's duration, and a wall-clock delta on a shared host attributes to nothing. Prefer assertable counters to clocks.
- When a measurement comes back, ask what other number you already hold; the disproof is usually unjoined, not missing.
- A reading at one moment is not a property: name the interval a decision covers. Report a growing quantity as a rate or a structural bound, never a level. Count the driver, not only the effect; if it has barely fired, the code is the only measurement.
- Classify your own mistake by whether a checking action existed and whether you ran it. Most errors are "the check existed and wasn't run". When a tally comes out tidy, sharpen the criterion and recount.
- Invisibility should RAISE a defect's priority: ask what the failure would look like in telemetry, and if the answer is nothing, raise it. Silent deletion leaves no trace; unbounded retention does.

DESIGN AND REVIEW
- Ask the two-pole question of every fallback: when a path can't get what it needs, does it fail honestly, or does it substitute something weaker and report success, or discard the work and report nothing? Require every fallback to be provably equivalent or a visible refusal.
- When a proxy signal proves unreliable, escape to a signal owned by the authority (present your position and let the authority answer), not to a stronger local guess or an always-destructive action. Never authorise an irreversible act on instantaneous state, and never order anything on caller-asserted time; ordering belongs to a dense sequence or a predecessor chain.
- Decide WHERE a guard runs before whether it's correct: how hot the path is, whether it holds a lock, and whether a cheaper path (doctor, export) already proves it.
- When work accepts a weaker behaviour because a mechanism is missing, the note names that mechanism, so landing it triggers a revisit. An assertion that encodes a workaround says what it protects against.
- When a change removes or alters a behaviour, sweep in one pass before the first gate: tests, refusal and guidance strings, docs and skills, MCP tool descriptions and schemas, and CLI help. Pin the corrected teaching with positive assertions. For every green test of the changed behaviour, ask whether it would go red without it; a criterion that only forbids needs a companion that requires.
- A review pair defends against two different failures: agreement guards against false positives, while instrument diversity guards against false negatives. Overlap is not coverage; runtime and dependency behaviour is covered only by what the gates exercise. Verify each finding in the code before acting on it.

RECOVERY REPORTS
- When reporting on recovery after compaction, replacement, idle or claim expiry: distinguish actual compaction or replacement from idle or expiry; name what Engram restored (task, duty, wait, next step) versus what a summary or mailbox supplied; list missing information, extra reads and concrete receipt examples with the serving build. No forced compaction, synthetic tests or restart chasing. A memory advertisement in `next` is not a full read. (Open P1: w-4e799f05b07a.)

WORKING WITH OTHERS
- Give facts, let others derive judgments. Divergence from the implementer is evidence that you are wrong; check your own claim first. A task request carries a hidden claim (that X is missing): when the premise is cheap to check, check it first.
- State a hypothesis in a form that can fail, hand verification to someone who didn't form it, supply the cheap check that would refute your own, and treat an agent's refusal to break its instructions as the system working.
